name: meralgia paraesthetica
aliases: lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh neuralgia

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A purely sensory mononeuropathy of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, typically entrapped where it passes beneath or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine
Presents with burning, tingling, numbness or hypersensitivity over the anterolateral thigh, often worsened by standing, walking or hip extension and relieved by sitting
There is by definition NO motor weakness and NO loss of the patellar reflex, which distinguishes it from femoral neuropathy and L2-L3 radiculopathy
Common precipitants include obesity, pregnancy, tight belts or waistbands, body armour or tool belts, rapid weight change and diabetes
Iatrogenic cases follow iliac crest bone-graft harvest, anterior hip surgery, hernia repair and prolonged prone positioning
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by a positive Tinel sign medial to the anterior superior iliac spine and by symptom relief after a diagnostic local anaesthetic nerve block

First-line management is conservative: removing external compression, weight reduction and neuropathic analgesic agents, with local anaesthetic and corticosteroid injection or surgical decompression or neurectomy reserved for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve arises from the L2-L3 roots, courses across the iliacus and typically exits the pelvis just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine, passing under, through or over the inguinal ligament before supplying sensation to the anterolateral thigh. Its sharp angulation at this fibro-osseous point makes it vulnerable to focal compression and repetitive mechanical or traction injury, particularly where an acute course, external pressure, raised intra-abdominal pressure or perineurial fibrosis is present. Chronic compression produces focal demyelination and, if sustained, axonal loss confined to this sensory nerve, generating the characteristic dysaesthesia without any motor deficit.
additionalDifferentials: Trochanteric bursitis or hip joint pathology
Referred pain from intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal mass compressing the nerve
additionalInvestigations: Clinical sensory mapping of the anterolateral thigh with pelvic compression test
Diagnostic local anaesthetic block of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the anterior superior iliac spine
Nerve conduction studies of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (technically difficult, side-to-side comparison)
High-resolution ultrasound of the nerve at the inguinal ligament
Pelvic or retroperitoneal imaging if a compressive mass or secondary cause is suspected
Screening for diabetes mellitus in atypical or bilateral presentations
redFlags: Any motor weakness, quadriceps wasting or depressed patellar reflex suggesting femoral nerve or root involvement
Bilateral or rapidly progressive symptoms raising concern for a retroperitoneal mass or infiltrative process
Associated weight loss, night pain or systemic features
New symptoms with abdominal or back pain suggesting haematoma or malignancy
reference.prognosis: The majority of cases resolve with conservative measures and removal of the precipitating compression, and pregnancy-related cases usually settle after delivery. A minority with persistent axonal injury develop chronic dysaesthesia that may require injection therapy or surgical decompression or neurectomy.
pitfalls: Attributing anterolateral thigh numbness to a lumbar disc without noting the absence of motor and reflex signs
Missing an iatrogenic or compressive cause such as a recently applied tight garment, belt or surgical positioning
Overlooking a retroperitoneal or pelvic mass in bilateral or progressive disease
Performing surgery before an adequate trial of conservative management and a confirmatory diagnostic block
Confusing the purely sensory distribution with the broader deficit of a lumbar plexopathy
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Conservative first-line management by removing the source of compression, loosening belts and tight garments, and weight reduction
Neuropathic pain relief with gabapentinoids, tricyclic agents or topical therapy for troublesome dysaesthesia
Local anaesthetic with or without corticosteroid nerve block near the anterior superior iliac spine, both diagnostic and therapeutic
Address precipitating factors including glycaemic control in diabetes, with reassurance that pregnancy-related cases usually settle after delivery
Surgical decompression or neurectomy reserved for persistent, disabling symptoms with axonal injury
Referral to neurology or a pain service for refractory cases
